clue.text: Best-laid plans (that is, what's expected to succeed)

definitions.text: Best-laid plans (that is, what's expected to succeed)

parts.note: surface: a phrase about carefully made schemes
setter's reading: the words that conventionally follow 'the best-laid plans' in the Burns proverb, and also a famous novel title

explanation.surface: A note on carefully drawn-up schemes and what is supposed to come of them.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns wrote of the best-laid schemes 'o' mice an' men'; the proverb runs 'the best-laid plans of mice and men', and Steinbeck took his title from it. 'Succeed' means follow in the phrase, not triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb's next words after the opening phrase are the Steinbeck novel title, so it literally comes after, succeeding the quoted words.

clue.text: Release, from loud wind instrument, a contemplative sound

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud
a reed is a pipe instrument blown with breath
the syllable chanted in meditation

explanation.surface: A musician coaxes a meditative note out of a loud woodwind.
explanation.definitionFit: Release as a noun means liberation from captivity, the state of being let go, which is a synonym.

clue.text: Exemption from prosecution right for nuclear pollution

indicators.note: one thing put in place of another: the first letter goes in where the second used to stand

parts.note: freedom from punishment or legal consequence
R is the abbreviation for right
N is the abbreviation for nuclear

explanation.surface: A legal note on immunity granted in a case about radioactive contamination.
explanation.walkthrough: IMPUNITY swaps its N for an R, giving IMPURITY.
explanation.definitionFit: An impurity is a contaminating substance mixed into something, so the word works as a synonym for pollution.

clue.text: Comfort to be found in tea set

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words rather than being built from their meanings

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Taking comfort from a nice tea service.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfort as a noun means a relaxed state free of strain or pain, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Half of lectures skipped after negative feedback's beginning: university student's remiss

indicators.note: only part of the word survives, and 'skipped' tells us the rest is dropped
skipping lectures means not attending, so the remaining part is missed out

parts.note: the standard short form of negative
the first half of the word, with the second half dropped

indicators.note: the start of a word is just its opening letter

parts.note: its opening letter
U is the abbreviation for university
L is a learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A student who cut classes after critical feedback is told off for laxity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the lectures piece after NEG. The final 's is 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone remiss fails to take proper care over duties, which is exactly what being neglectful means.

clue.text: Languidly moved bike

definitions.meaning: first meaning: wandered about listlessly, as if sulking
second meaning: a small motorised two-wheeler with pedals

explanation.surface: Someone pushed a bicycle along in a lazy, listless way.
explanation.definitionFit: As a past-tense verb it means drifted around aimlessly, and as a noun it names a low-powered motorcycle.

clue.text: Largely unnecessary heckles

indicators.note: most but not all of the word is kept, so its final letter goes

parts.note: without any need, superfluous

explanation.surface: A complaint that most interruptions from the audience were uncalled for.
explanation.definitionFit: To heckle is to taunt and provoke, and as verbs the answer means irritates or goads someone in the same way.

clue.text: Gather up old lamps to collect mint in long-running TV show

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to net is to gather in, as a catch
O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: collecting something means taking it inside, so one piece holds another

parts.note: both are slang verbs meaning hits or punches
in mint condition means brand new

explanation.surface: Someone collects antique lamps and coins, a scene from a long-running TV programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamps' is a verb here: British slang for punches, and 'clocks' is slang for the same. The answer is a long-running British evening news bulletin.
explanation.definitionFit: The late-evening bulletin on British television has been broadcast for decades, so it is a fair example of a long-running programme.

clue.text: Novel, starting point for film

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so these letters are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A book that served as the source for a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' wants to be the definition, since the film came from Irvine Welsh's book; it is the anagram signal, and 'film' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Danny Boyle's 1996 movie about Edinburgh heroin users bears this title, so it is a specific example of a film.

clue.text: Former European politican talks emptily, making excuses

parts.note: ex- means former
E is the abbreviation for European
a Member of Parliament; the clue's spelling is as printed

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its insides, leaving only the outside pair

parts.note: just its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A former Euro MP talks a lot of hot air while making excuses.
explanation.definitionFit: To excuse someone from a duty or rule is to release them from it, which is what the verb exempt means.

clue.text: Time out before study in space age unit

parts.note: a gap is an empty space
ages are counted in years

explanation.surface: A break before college spent in the space age.
explanation.walkthrough: A gap year is the British term for a year off, often travelling, between school and university.
explanation.definitionFit: Students take this break from education, usually between school and university, so it is time off before further study.

clue.text: King rode off before giving command

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled or gone wrong, so these letters are scrambled into a new arrangement

parts.note: R is Rex, Latin for king
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monarch rides away before issuing an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A command is an authoritative instruction, and an order is the same thing given by someone in charge.

clue.text: Was familiar with where to buy cold meats: they say, in a big city

indicators.note: what people say is heard, not read, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: past tense of to know
a delicatessen sells sliced cold meats

explanation.surface: Someone knew the local shop for sliced ham in a large city.
explanation.definitionFit: India's capital is one of the world's largest metropolitan areas, so calling it a big city is fair.

clue.text: Oversees 'Pies Versus Stew'

indicators.note: a stew is a jumble of things cooked together, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone judges a contest between pastry dishes and casseroles.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a cookery contest; 'Stew' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee is to watch over and direct work, which is a close synonym of manage or monitor here.

clue.text: Lecturer with big book about gravy boat culture finally finds desired piece of terminology

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for lecturer

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a tome is a large heavy volume
jus is thin meat gravy, from the French

indicators.note: the end of each of the two words is all that is used

parts.note: the final letter of each word

explanation.surface: A lecturer with a fat volume on gravy boats is hunting for just the right word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins L to the reversed book.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means the exact right word, the precise term a writer is searching for.

clue.text: What an employer does is manipulates

definitions.meaning: first meaning: employs, puts staff or tools to work
second meaning: exploits someone for one's own ends

explanation.surface: A cynical remark that bosses exploit their workers.
explanation.definitionFit: An employer employs, a synonym; and to exploit a person selfishly is another sense of the same verb.

clue.text: Salem's gone berserk: an Arthur Miller play's subject

indicators.note: running wild and out of control, so these letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Salem, setting of The Crucible, runs amok, as in a Miller play.
explanation.walkthrough: Salem's witch-hunt hysteria is the setting of Miller's The Crucible, which makes 'gone berserk' fit; the answer comes from his other famous play.
explanation.definitionFit: Willy Loman, the hero of Miller's Death of a Salesman, is a travelling commercial representative, the play's central figure.

clue.text: Care of company address for Chanel

parts.note: c/o, as written on an envelope
Co. is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: An envelope addressed to the fashion designer via her firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabrielle Chanel, the French fashion designer, was universally known by this nickname as her first name.

clue.text: Wimbledon champ, bully, gets easy money

parts.note: Pat Cash, the Australian who won the men's title in 1987
to cow is to intimidate

explanation.surface: A tennis champion who throws their weight around makes money effortlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: A business or product that keeps producing profit with little effort is called this, an idiom for reliable income.

clue.text: Outfit with attempt to convey 'pizazz'

parts.note: a get-up is a set of clothes, often eye-catching
and means together with
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Trying to show flair with a striking costume.
explanation.definitionFit: Pizazz is energetic flair and liveliness, and the hyphenated phrase means drive and enthusiasm, a near synonym.

clue.text: Taj Mahal's setting captured in simple drawing

indicators.note: something captured is held inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: dim means slow-witted
the Indian city where the monument stands

explanation.surface: A basic sketch of the Taj Mahal and its surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple' looks like an adjective for the drawing; it is DIM, meaning not bright.
explanation.definitionFit: A schematic picture showing how something is laid out is a kind of drawing, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Dramatic drop in bill at seedy bar

parts.note: a bird's bill is its beak, slang for nose
a dive is a disreputable drinking place

explanation.surface: The tab at a grotty pub suddenly falls sharply.
explanation.definitionFit: A plunge, of an aircraft or of prices, is a steep sudden fall, matching a dramatic drop.

clue.text: Naiad, fabulous goddess

indicators.note: fabulous means fictional or invented, so the letters are made up into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A water nymph described as a wonderful deity of legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' looks like praise or a word for mythical; it is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman deity of hunting and the moon is a classical goddess, so the answer is an example.

clue.text: Conservative pursues cut back, at first taking on the money

indicators.note: following on behind means the first piece is placed after the reversed word
going back means the word runs right to left

parts.note: to axe is to cut
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter is used

parts.note: its opening letter

explanation.surface: A Tory follows budget cuts by grabbing the cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on the money is precisely right, the idiom meaning spot-on, a match for the adjective.

clue.text: Said what you might find on collar of Siamese

indicators.note: something said is spoken aloud, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.words: what you might find on collar
parts.note: a necktie is worn round a shirt collar

explanation.surface: Speculation about what is on a Siamese cat's collar.
explanation.walkthrough: Siamese suggests the cat, whose collar might carry a tag; here it is the people of Siam, now Thailand.
explanation.definitionFit: Siam is the old name of Thailand, so a Siamese person or thing is from that country.

clue.text: They might spell trouble, 200 wains

indicators.note: trouble suggests disorder and upset, so these letters are thrown around

parts.note: taken as written; wains are farm wagons
CC is 200 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A warning that a couple of hundred farm carts could mean bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell trouble' reads as a phrase meaning herald problems; split it so 'They might spell' is the definition. The CC goes in among the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of modern witchcraft religion cast charms and incantations, so they are people who might cast a spell.

clue.text: Sporting achievement in show

parts.note: someone who is in is at home
to run a story or programme is to show it

explanation.surface: A sporting triumph displayed in an exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word; it is the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball, hitting the ball so the batter circles every base to score is a celebrated feat of the game.

clue.text: Sh! The man I saw crawling around — you know… thingummy…

indicators.note: creeping about in every direction means the letters move out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone whispers about a man they saw creeping about but cannot recall his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are placeholder words used when a speaker cannot remember a particular person's or thing's name.
